replies.author: RobodOfficial
replies.body:
That’s a fair point. A lot of strategies look impressive in backtests but fall apart in live markets once fees, slippage, and changing market conditions come into play.  
I think the bigger problem isn’t finding another AI trading tool. It’s learning how to properly validate a strategy before trusting it with real money. A profitable backtest alone doesn’t prove anything.  
But here’s something worth thinking about. If someone spends months researching, testing, and building something useful, and the moment they share it, we call it advertising, what exactly are we expecting them to do?  
And if we’re asking people to share their hard-earned knowledge and strategies, shouldn’t we also ask what we’re bringing to the table?  
There’s a big difference between empty promotion and someone genuinely trying to solve a problem. Both shouldn’t be treated the same way.  
Skepticism is healthy. Dismissing everything as advertising isn’t always fair either.

replies.body: I don’t necessarily believe that to be true. I’ve built a trading bot and it’s just past its first eval. It’s taken almost a full year to get to this point it’s not as black and white as lots of people make it out to be. I too struggle to find anyone else in the same space who’s willing to talk about it in depth but i’m sure there are people out there who won’t just hand out minimal advice. What is it you are stuck on specifically. My biggest hurdle was looking for edges. Test after test after test i’d get nothing back. It was insanely discouraging but then i thought about other bases to explore. You don’t need one BIG edge. You can find multiple smaller one and leverage them together. Do they have a relation, when market does x what happens to the other small edge. Every output creates a bigger pucture

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
I Fair, and good to hear from someone who actually stuck with it for a year. "Test after test, nothing back" is exactly where I've been, so I get the discouraging part.

Curious what the first eval was. A prop firm challenge, or your own out-of-sample test? How many trades did it cover, and on what market? I ask because I've had things pass a short window and then fall apart on data they'd never seen, so now I only trust a pass when I know how long and how independent the test was.

On stacking smaller edges, I agree in principle, it's how the big shops do it. The catch I keep running into: stacking only helps if each small edge is real on its own. If they aren't, adding five of them just gives you five pieces of noise that look like a portfolio. The other trap is correlation. Things that look unrelated in normal months tend to move together exactly when the market breaks. Did you check how your pieces behave together in the bad weeks?

Happy to compare notes in DMs if you're up for it. Methods and the dead ends, not anyone's live settings.

replies.author: qzy4628
replies.body: I believe it really comes down to the way you are testing. It’s super tricky to get right because you want to validate enough to get rid of luck, noise and false winners but then not too much to remove real edges. Testing in sample out of sample, forward testing etc help but the structure of the rules are a big part of it too. To be honest sometimes you don’t even need an edge, just build the right framework to your targeted propfirm. It’s very subjective to your system though.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I can't speak to anyone's live results, but one thing that helps is to have the AI write the rules and let a separate test judge them. Check the result after fees and keep some recent data you never tuned on, because AI-built strategies often look great on the data they were built from. Start small or in paper mode before real money. Cymetica's Backtest Labs includes fees and can hold out the last part of the history for that kind of check.

replies.author: Muschnick
replies.body:
I 2nd that, I have a jury of codex/gemini/grok and Claude main agent that proposes the moves and does the research. 

I would love to figure out a good back and forth between agents where they are all researching and coming up with proposals to buy and the jury of agents votes.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: A jury is a nice idea. One thing to watch is that models trained on similar data can agree on the same mistake, so a unanimous vote isn't always safer. I'd have each agent give its answer before seeing the others, and give them different jobs or data, like one only arguing against the trade. Then track every vote against what actually happened, so you can see which agents earn a say and which don't.

comments.author: Illustrious-King-83
comments.body:
Depends what you mean.....  do you mean using AI to write the code for a strategy you already have in mind  or are already trading ?  or do you mean feeding a load of information  to Claude  every hour and asking if you should buy or sell ?    or do you mean some sort of combo of the 2 ?     

from experience,  and from the other answers,  I'd say 1) AI can help you code a strategy in python / pinescript etc, IF you already  have specific ideas but  if you ask it for a strategy its going to give something generic, which probably wouldn't work.  if you are directly giving it information about a stock /indices and asking buy or sell,  then...... honestly I have no idea,  I've written something like that. but  its hard to backtest,  and you can only forward test  it on a demo account, and ur gonna spend alot of tokens and time doing that.  there are a few GitHub repos that setup a number of agents that form a "hedge fund"   it looks pretty interesting... but again ur might burn alot of tokens to find out it doesn't work. 

The other  use is if you have an idea is using the AI to fill it out, but again I've done that and you can end up going down a rabbit hole and spend days trying something that doesn't work.....  

Theres alot of stuff on YouTube about it,  but honestly  they make money from clicks and engagement  not because the AI bots are profitable

comments.author: eduard_trades
comments.body:
I've been running trading agents on crypto prop accounts for a few months, built with Claude Code. Honest summary: AI made me much faster at building, and it didn't give me an edge.



What worked:

\- The LLM never decides entries. A fixed, rule-based strategy does. Claude writes and audits the code around it: risk limits, stop handling, reconciliation with the exchange.

\- An audit that compares the code against the firm's published rules, line by line. Mine found that the bot implemented a static daily limit where the firm uses a trailing one. The code ran fine. It was just the wrong rule.



What didn't:

\- The backtest. A bug in how exits were filled made the strategy look profitable. Fixed, it came out around zero after fees.

\- Asking the model for strategy ideas. You get textbook setups.



If you're building one: paper first like you plan, and before trusting any result, check it against random entries with the same exits and costs.

comments.author: Monsterdesk_ai
comments.body: I’m building one too, and my most useful finding wasn’t a strategy, it was a testing rule: never judge a bot on data it was tuned on. When I audited mine, most of the “unseen” test days had already been used to pick the winners. After I fixed that and charged realistic costs per trade, most of my agents stopped passing. What survived were plain, slow rules with few settings. So whatever you build, hold back a stretch of data until the very end, charge real costs, and run it on paper for a few weeks before trusting any backtest number.

All jokes aside tho, if you're building a bot off LLMs just keep your expectations super low. the api wrappers are great for writing boilerplate python or debugging pandas, but if you let the model make actual trading decisions it'll find some overfitted backtest pattern and convince you you're a genius right before wiping your account.
